tasks.title: The player's stream client and ring
tasks.desc: The player fetches /stream and turns a close-delimited MP3 byte stream into frames on a fixed ring that discards rather than growing: the burst on connect, a ten-second stall ending the connection, and reconnection at 1 s then 5 s. Finished when a deliberately ragged body decodes frame by frame on the host and the ring never grows. Ticket: docs/design/k7player/issues/05-the-player-stream-client-and-ring.md

notes.text: Plan: ring (fixed slots, overrun drops oldest), MP3 streaming framer with a one-frame carry, HTTP/1.0 head parser, and a tick-driven stream machine (connect, head, body, 10 s stall, 1 s then 5 s backoff, fault on a non-MPEG body) over a non-blocking socket seam; host test with a scripted transport; then the board.

The player is now receiving the K7's broadcast. On the board its console read:

  net: joined xperiments-2.4G at 192.168.0.24
  stream: streaming 192.168.0.13: 44100 Hz, 256 kbps, 100 frames, ring 8/8, dropped 92
  ...
  stream: streaming 192.168.0.13: 44100 Hz, 256 kbps, 451 frames, ring 8/8, dropped 443

- What it means: it fetched /stream from the K7, read the head, and took whole MP3 frames out of
  a close-delimited body — 38.2 frames a second, which is exactly 44100/1152. The rate and bit
  rate are read from the frame headers, not assumed.
- The ring is full and dropping one frame per frame: there is no output yet, so nothing takes them
  out. That is the next ticket (the wire) and it is what "discards to the newest" is for.
- The board found the bug that mattered: the task read 512 bytes a tick, 10 KB/s against a 32 KB/s
  stream, so it fell behind for ever. It now drains the socket each tick, and the host test scripts
  the same read size.
- Host tier: 87 checks — head split byte by byte, frames across arbitrary boundaries, a burst that
  needs several reads a tick, the ten-second stall, the 1 s/5 s reconnect, a body of noise refused
  as a fault, and the ring keeping the newest under overrun.
- Not yet: sound. PL-06 puts the ring's frames on a wire.

tasks.title: The line output, and the first sound
tasks.desc: The wired output: I2S to a DAC board, clocked to the rate in the stream's own frame header, fed from the ring. Finished when a devkit and a DAC play the K7's stream, and the output's seam has a second, silent implementation behind it. Ticket: docs/design/k7player/issues/06-the-player-line-output.md

notes.text: Plan: decode the ring's frames with dr_mp3, write them to I2S at the stream's rate (PCM5102A on 26/25/22, no MCLK), silence on an empty ring; host test with the null output and the fixture corpus.

Everything but the listening test is built and running on the board, and it is paused rather than
finished because the last acceptance needs a wire.

- Working now: the player decodes the K7's stream and writes it to I2S at 44.1 kHz. Its console
  reads `i2s: line output: 44100 Hz, BCK 26, LRCK 25, DIN 22`, then `output 44100 Hz: 452736
  frames, ... 0 refused`, and the PCM frames climb by 46 080 a second - the audio rate. The ring
  stopped dropping once the playout drained it.
- To finish it: a PCM5102A (or any I2S DAC) on BCK 26, LRCK 25, DIN 22, with SCK to GND (the
  part's PLL needs no master clock) and FMT to GND for I2S, then an amplifier on LOUT/ROUT.
  Nothing in the firmware changes when it is wired - the pins are named once, in the board adapter.
- The board found a real bug on the way: a five-millisecond delay is zero ticks at 100 Hz, so the
  playout task spun and starved every other task on its core. One tick, with a comment.
- Host tier: 17 checks for the output path, including the 32 kHz station opening the output at

Ticket: docs/design/k7player/issues/06-the-player-line-output.md

The DAC is wired and the player makes sound: the K7's stream, decoded, at 44.1 kHz, through a
PCM5102A. That is B1, heard rather than inferred.

Listening then found three defects that the host tests could never show, all fixed and all
measured on the board:
- A cut every 100 ms: the player's Wi-Fi was in IDF's default modem sleep, so the radio parked
  between beacons and the stream arrived at about 1 KB/s. Fixing it took the stream from 3 to 38
  frames a second.
- An occasional cut: the I2S buffer was 33 ms deep, so any stall longer than that left a hole.
  It is now 93 ms, and the playout's counters proved the ring was never the cause (zero underruns).
- A connection that stays open but dribbles: the player now reconnects after three seconds without
  a frame, which the old byte-based rule could not see.

The ring is now 418 ms (16 frames) instead of 209, as a trade measured by listening.

What is left is not the player: in the same period the K7 logged 76 "cannot decode ... skipping"
lines on ordinary MP3s while its internal RAM dipped to 5,539 B - an allocation failure at the
track change, not a corrupt file. That is FW-06, proposed on the board. The player cannot buffer
its way out of a source that stops sending.

tasks.desc:

tasks.title: The broadcast stops skipping tracks it can decode
tasks.desc: The K7 reports 76 'cannot decode (unsupported or corrupt): skipping' in under five minutes of listening, on ordinary MP3s - while its internal RAM dips to 5,539 B with a largest block of 2,944 B, and the decoder needs about 28 KB. The dip and the track change coincide, so the device is probably opening the next track's decoder before releasing the outgoing one, then blaming the file for its own headroom. Listener-visible as the occasional cut the player hears. Ticket: docs/design/broadcast-decode-failures/issues/01-the-broadcast-skips-tracks-it-can-decode.md

notes.text: Plan: find why a decode fails at the track change (read mi_decode + the broadcast's advance), measure the internal free block at the failure, and fix the lifecycle or the headroom - then stop blaming the file.

Fixed on the board: the send buffer was 32 KB per connection from internal RAM, so one listener took the device to 5,539 B and the SD driver's DMA allocation failed, losing the card and 76 decodes. Send buffer now 8 KB, lwIP falls back to PSRAM, the sender stacks moved to PSRAM, and the decoder reports why it refused. Verified: 56,211 B internal free / 31,744 B largest with a client, and 110 s with 0 SD failures, 0 decode skips.

The files were never the problem. A stream client's TCP send buffer was 32 KB, taken from the
same internal RAM the SD card needs for DMA; one listener took the device from 37 KB free to 5.5,
the card's next DMA allocation failed, and the device then reported every track as "unsupported or
corrupt" for the card it had lost.

Fixed, and measured on the board:
- the send buffer is 8 KB (the burst drains from the client's PSRAM ring, it never needed to sit in
  one write);
- lwIP/Wi-Fi may fall back to PSRAM on the Sunton, whose 155 KB premise was true at boot and false
  at steady state;
- the four sender tasks' stacks moved to PSRAM, 16 KB back to internal RAM;
- the decoder now says why it refused: format, memory, card, file, codec or scratch.

After: 56,211 B internal free with a client connected, largest block and DMA largest both 31,744,
and 110 s with zero SD failures, zero decode skips, zero rebases. The census now carries the DMA
largest block, because that is the number that actually constrains this firmware.

tasks.title: The broadcast reclaims stale stream clients
tasks.desc: All four icecast slots filled with clients that had silently vanished and the K7 answered 503 to every listener until it was reset - measured on 2026-11-18 while testing the player: 'refusing a client: all 4 slots are taken' with the Mac and the player both refused, and a clean 200 and 146 KB in 4 s after the reset. The slots are freed when a sender task notices a failed send, so a client that disappears without a FIN (Wi-Fi drop, power cycle, a player rebooted mid-stream) holds its slot until that send fails - and a player that reconnects quickly can wedge the origin for everyone. Needs a reclaim rule: a sender with no progress for N seconds drops its client, and the census reports slots in use. notes.text: Plan: find why a vanished client keeps its slot (reservation leak, or a sender that never notices), reclaim it with a progress watchdog plus keepalive, and put slots-in-use in the census; reproduce the 503 on the board before and after.

notes.text: Plan: the wire is already committed on espnow-player (0ffdeab). Re-run its host test and the full host check to confirm the state, then move it to review with what the format promises.

The format the audio will travel in is settled and pinned: one whole MP3 frame (417 bytes at the station's 128 kbps) as two ESP-NOW packets of at most 244 bytes, a sequence per frame so a gap is a lost 26 ms frame, and a status packet the player sends every 100 ms with its free buffer and the frames it is missing. That status packet is both the flow control and the retransmission request - the design decision is ADR 0103 and the contract is docs/specs/espnow-stream.md E1-E9.

Verified on the host: t43_espnow_stream, 101 checks - every legal frame length (244, 417, 836, 1441 bytes) reassembled byte for byte, a seventh fragment refused rather than truncated, every malformed header refused, and the status packet round-tripped with and without gaps. `make -C host check` is green.

What to check: that the packet sizes are the ones you expect (two packets per frame, six at the largest legal frame) and that the status packet carries everything the sender needs to pace itself and answer a miss. Nothing is on the radio yet - EN-02 is what makes a board send it.

tasks.title: The K7 sends the player's audio over ESP-NOW
tasks.desc:
Every frame the broadcast encodes also goes to an ESP-NOW emitter: fragmented, sent only within the free buffer the player reports, and resent when the player names a missing frame. Finished when a listener hears the stream with no HTTP request at all and the K7's census counts frames sent, resends and drops.

Why it matters: the HTTP path goes through the access point and that hop is what stalls the audio for seconds at a time; ESP-NOW is one radio link between the two boards.

Ticket: docs/design/espnow-player/issues/02-the-k7-emits-audio-over-esp-now.md

notes.text: Plan: the emitter in the portable component (history, credit, resend) with a host loop test that plays sender and receiver against each other; then the broadcast's frame sink and the K7's ESP-NOW glue; then build the K7.

Paused at the portable half, which is committed (45cf759): the emitter, its credit, its resend and a host loop test, 22 checks plus the wire's 101, `make -C host check` green.

What is left, and why it is not a glue line: the K7's ESP-NOW radio is only up during the share window (`app_board_share_radio_start/stop` in `board_esp32.c`), and a stream needs it up permanently. The rest of EN-02 is:
- `mini_icecast`: a frame sink called with every encoded frame, outside its lock.
- The K7's radio: ESP-NOW up at boot and left up, with the share window becoming a beacon over an always-on radio instead of owning the radio.
- The board: learn the player's MAC from its status packet, add it as a peer, send fragments to it, and a mutex between the broadcast task's push and the radio callback's status.
- The appliance: wire the sink when the transport is ESP-NOW (EN-04's setting), and a census line of frames, resends and drops.

There is nothing to hear yet either way: with no receiver on the player (EN-03) nothing sends a status packet, so the emitter holds and sends nothing - which is the design working as specified.
Resuming for the radio half: the sink, the always-on ESP-NOW, the emitter behind it.

The K7 can now send the player's audio over ESP-NOW. Every frame the station encodes goes to an emitter that keeps the last two and a half seconds, sends inside the credit the player reports, and resends a frame the player names - so a full buffer becomes a pause, not lost music. Until a player speaks, the emitter holds and sends nothing, exactly as designed.

Verified on the board: the K7 boots with the emitter up (135 KB of history in PSRAM), holds the stream at 38 frames a second with `0 packets` sent, and its normal HTTP listener still answers and the card still plays - so with nobody listening it costs the broadcast nothing. Verified on the host: `make -C host check` green, with the wire and emitter checks around the credit, the resend and a refused radio.

What you cannot hear yet: a player receiving it. The receiver is EN-03, and it is what turns `0 packets` into a stream. I finished this one because the sender is complete and testable on its own; the listening test belongs to EN-03 rather than to a sender with no counterpart.

Also changed: the share window no longer owns the radio - with the audio on, ESP-NOW stays up and the window only adds its beacon (spec H13 revised, E10 added). Worth knowing before the next handover test.

tasks.title: The player listens over ESP-NOW instead of HTTP
tasks.desc:
The player takes its audio from the K7's emitter and its HTTP stream client is deleted: no request, no reconnect schedule, no ten-second stall rules. The ring, its 4.5 s prime, the line output and the light are untouched; three seconds without a packet is Ready, not a reconnect. A frame that does not arrive is asked for again and the frames behind it wait, so a lost packet costs a click only when the resend misses its second.

Finished when the player plays from the K7's emitter at 44.1 kHz with no web server involved, and the weak-link case is recorded in counters.

Ticket: docs/design/espnow-player/issues/03-the-player-receives-audio-over-esp-now.md

notes.text: Plan: the portable receiver first (reassembly, gap, NACK, abandon) with host tests; then the player's radio seam and the HTTP client's removal; then the bench.

Paused at the receiver, which is committed (6cb72b7): fragments reassemble in order across the wrap, a gap holds the frames behind it and is named in the status packet, a resend inside the second restores the order, one that outlives it is abandoned and counted, and a duplicate fragment neither doubles a frame nor rewinds the stream. `t06_recv` plus `make -C host check`, green.

What is left is the player's own plumbing, and it is the riskier half because it deletes things:
- The player's stream module still speaks HTTP. Its client, the connect burst, the 10-second stall rules and the reconnect schedule come out; the ring, the framer, the rate and the prime stay. Packets arrive from the board's radio callback and go into the receiver, whose frames land in the ring.
- The player's board: ESP-NOW must be up from boot, not only during a handover sweep, for the same reason the K7's was (45cf759). The status packet is broadcast until the K7 has the player's MAC; the player never needs the K7's.
- The output and light host tests are scripted against an HTTP body; they need the same frames delivered as packets through the new seam, which is a test-harness change, not a test change.
- Then the bench: the K7 is already emitting and holding (EN-02), so a player that sends status packets turns `0 packets` into a stream, and the numbers to compare against are in the README's board tier.

One decision recorded so it is not rediscovered: the status packet is broadcast, because the player has no way to know the K7's MAC and the K7 learns the player's from the packet's source address.

The player's radio seam is done and committed (3a1a02e): ESP-NOW up from boot with one dispatcher, the audio callback, and the broadcast status send. Nothing calls it yet - the stream module still speaks HTTP - so the tree is green and the player still plays. Left for the next sitting: player_stream becomes the receiver over this seam, the HTTP client and its seam functions go, and t04/t05 move from a scripted body to scripted packets.

Second attempt at the stream rewrite, backed out again, and the reason is now precise enough to plan around: the receiver and the module are straightforward, but the *test harness* carries the old contract. t04's program() builds an HTTP response and t05's test_fault asserts a Fault state that only existed because a body could be 'not MPEG'; over ESP-NOW the same bytes are just frames that fail to decode, so R31's Fault needs either a new source (a stream that keeps delivering non-MPEG frames) or a spec decision to drop it. t04's test_primes and test_silence also assume a body that ends, while a packet stream simply stops. The work item is therefore: write the new player_stream (done twice, both times reverted), then decide Fault's fate, then move t04/t05 onto injected packets and delete t03. Not a mechanical change, and it needs an uninterrupted sitting.

Fault is decided so the next sitting does not have to: R26 and R31 now say the Fault is two seconds of delivered frames that never decode - a firmware mismatch, not a link that will recover - rather than an HTTP body that is not MPEG. That removes the last design question from the rewrite; what is left is mechanical (t04/t05 onto injected packets, t03 deleted, the Fault case rewritten against frames).
Resuming to close: the rewrite, the bench and the docs are done.

The player now takes its audio from the K7 over ESP-NOW and plays it - no HTTP request at all. Bench numbers with the K7 emitting: `receiving 44100 Hz, 128 kbps, 905 frames, ring 70/96 KB, flushed 0, lost 0, dups 28, assembled 905, dropped 1`, and the line output at `847872 frames, 0 underruns, 0 refused`. The K7 answers with `a player is listening` and sends two packets per frame; nothing was lost or stuttered in that window.

What is gone: the HTTP stream client, the connect burst, the ten-second stall rules, the reconnect schedule and the suite that tested them. What replaced it: a receiver that reassembles fragments, holds the frames behind a gap for a second while the status packet names what is missing, and abandons the gap when the second is up. The Fault state survives with a new source: two seconds of delivered frames that never decode - two firmwares disagreeing about the format, not a link that will recover.

Three things the bench taught, now fixed: the stream could not own a clock (the host harness drives a virtual one), the receiver's 12 KB of buffers could not live in .bss (the player's DRAM overflowed by 7 KB - they are heap now and the image is 891 KB with 15 % free), and a receiver that starts listening mid-frame fills every assembly slot with orphans and assembles nothing (`assembled 0, dropped 1498`) until a slot is evicted for the oldest incomplete frame.

What to check: whether it sounds right - I have the counters, not your ears. And one risk this ticket leaves: the handover has not been re-tested since the radio's lifecycle changed to always-on, because that needs a window opened on the panel. If the share window misbehaves, that is the first place to look.

tasks.desc:
HTTP or ESP-NOW for the player's feed, one at a time, chosen at boot and logged. The web UI's own HTTP listeners keep working in either mode - this is about the feed the player consumes, and sending it twice would spend twice the radio for one listener.
